title: Axolotls: The Smiling Salamander from Mexico
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum), a neotenic salamander from Mexico. They cover the Nahuatl name and the god Xolotl, Aztec lore and food/medicine uses, the natural habitat in Lake Xochimilco (and the remnant Lake Xochimilco area) and Lake Texcoco history, neoteny and why they keep larval traits, their colorful captive morphs, regeneration abilities and the blastema, the large genome, cancer resistance, lab-animal history, critical endangerment from habitat loss, pollution and invasive carp and tilapia, conservation efforts, their appearance on the Mexican 50-peso bill, and pet care tips. The episode closes with listener mail correcting the pronunciation of the name Bede.

segments.title: Opening banter and axolotl name origins
segments.summary: Hosts open the show and credit listener Charlie's Flores for preliminary research. They explain the pronunciation and Nahuatl origin of the name axolotl, its link to the god Xolotl, and the Lake Texcoco and Lake Xochimilco habitat history.

segments.title: Amphibian classification and neoteny
segments.summary: The axolotl's scientific name Ambystoma mexicanum is discussed, along with amphibian metamorphosis. The hosts explain neoteny, where axolotls keep larval traits such as gills and fins and can reproduce as adults, with a theory about their evolutionary history.

segments.title: Colors, appearance, and diet
segments.summary: Captive axolotls are bred in colors such as pink, white, and glow-in-the-dark varieties that do not occur in the wild, which are dark brownish or black. Their size, feathery external gills, and carnivorous nocturnal diet are described.

segments.title: Axolotl reproduction and lifespan
segments.summary: The mating waltz, egg counts of roughly 300 to 1,000, and hatch rates are discussed. Lifespan in captivity (up to about 25 years) and in the wild (about 10 to 15 years) is covered.

segments.title: Limb and organ regeneration
segments.summary: Stephanie Roy's research is quoted on axolotls regenerating limbs, spinal cords, and organs without scarring. The blastema, stem-cell-like differentiation, and the large axolotl genome are discussed, along with a cannibalism theory for the evolution of regeneration.

segments.title: Organ transplant and cancer resistance
segments.summary: Axolotls are described as accepting transplanted organs without rejection and as highly resistant to cancer. Research on breast cancer patients treated with axolotl egg serum is described.

segments.title: Lab animal history and research contributions
segments.summary: Axolotls were taken to France in the 19th century and became a lab animal, with the pink morphs descended from a small number of originals. Their large cells and eggs make them useful for study, and research has informed understanding of organ development and spina bifida.

segments.title: Endangerment and conservation
segments.summary: Axolotls are critically endangered in the wild due to habitat loss, pollution, and introduced carp and tilapia. Population numbers fell sharply since 1998. Captive axolotls cannot simply be released, and conservation efforts include sheltered breeding areas and designation as a flagship species.

segments.title: Culture: 50 peso bill, emoji, and Minecraft
segments.summary: The axolotl appears on the back of the Mexican 50-peso bill introduced in 2020, and Mexico City created an axolotl emoji in 2017. Chuck mentions axolotls appear in Minecraft.

segments.title: Axolotl pet care
segments.summary: Care tips include fresh filtered water kept at 60 to 64 degrees Fahrenheit with neutral pH, using a net instead of handling, live or carefully sourced food, a 20-gallon tank for one animal, and sand rather than gravel as substrate. The hosts credit the Atlantic City Aquarium.

segments.title: Show credits and 99% Invisible reference
segments.summary: Hosts thank contributors and mention the 99% Invisible episode Model Organism, which also covers axolotls.

segments.title: Listener mail: pronunciation of Bede
segments.summary: A listener from Wollongong, Australia, named Bede, corrects the hosts on the pronunciation of Saint Bede, the English scholar from Jarrow who wrote a history of the English people. The hosts discuss the pronunciation and sign off with the email address.
